articles.title: Taylor Swift Fires Up Academy Gala With Four Songs in Her First Band Performance Since the Eras Tour
articles.summary: Taylor Swift got some of the old gang back together for her first full-band performance since the Eras Tour, delivering a four-song set to a black-tie audience Saturday night at the Academy Museum 6th Annual Gala.
body: As expected, she also sang her contender for the 2027 Oscars, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” from the Pixar film “Toy Story 5.” It wasn’t her first live performance ever of that song — she did it at the Grammy Museum and at a private Ross House FYC showcase — but it was her first time singing it live with a full band, and not as part of a mash-up. Besides its Oscar eligibility, the song is also in contention at the Grammys, entered in the song of the year category as well as film soundtrack and country divisions.
For the remaining two slots in her set, Swift dug farther back into the past, covering both her cynical and romantic bases, opening with “Blank Space” and ending with “Love Story.”
Wearing a Ralph Lauren gown for her performance, Swift invited the formally clad gathering to dance along with her set, saying, “Dancing is absolutely allowed. It’s not mandatory, but it’s more fun.”

articles.title: Woodstock Film Festival Names Jessica Edwards as Executive Director
articles.summary: Jessica Edwards has been named the new executive director of the Woodstock Film Festival, the organization announced Sunday as the 27th annual festival came to a close. Edwards will take over the role from Meira Blaustein, the festival’s co-founder.
body: “From our very first meeting with Jessica, it was clear to us that she was the natural person to succeed Meira and carry forward the extraordinary work Meira has done over more than 25 years,” she said. “Jessica understands what makes the Woodstock Film Festival special — its commitment to filmmakers, its independent spirit, and its deep connection to the Hudson Valley — while also bringing the experience, energy, and vision to lead it into its next chapter. On behalf of the Board, we are tremendously excited to welcome Jessica as our new Executive Director, and to work with her on the future of the Festival.”

articles.title: Ali G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’
articles.summary: Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two.
body: “Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.”

At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film was Chicken Shop Date, which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.

Now that we have established I am not in fact Amelia Dimoldenberg – and that any boning today will be strictly chicken-related – Ali changes tack. Whenever anyone comes near our table, he loudly explains, to my embarrassment, that we are actually conducting a major drug deal. Having seemingly worked his way through the entire menu, he starts asking what else he would need to buy to get the bill up to £500, after discovering that the Guardian is footing it.

articles.title: Betty McGuire, Actress on Broadway and ‘Growing Pains,’ Dies at 100
articles.summary: She worked alongside Ethel Merman, Bea Arthur and Susan Hayward on the stage, was Joanna Kerns’ mom on the ABC sitcom and played a nun in ‘Up in Smoke.’
body: Betty McGuire, who appeared three times on Broadway and recurred as the mother of Joanna Kerns’ Maggie Seaver on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, has died. She was 100.

McGuire died Oct. 8 of natural causes at the Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital in Woodland Hills, close family friend Keith Gerchak, an actor and co-founder of Double G Films, told The Hollywood Reporter.
In 1978 films, she portrayed Sister Mary Quacker in Cheech & Chong’s Up in Smoke and a nurse in the Michael Crichton medical thriller Coma, starring Geneviève Bujold.

Born on March 20, 1926, in Bridgeport, Connecticut, McGuire performed and understudied on Broadway alongside the likes of Ethel Merman, Barbara Cook, Bea Arthur and Tony Randall in the original productions of the musicals Plain and Fancy in 1955-56, Happy Hunting in 1956-57 and Oh, Captain! in 1958.

articles.title: Why M. Bison From Street Fighter (2026) Looks So Familiar
articles.summary: The 2026 Street Fighter movie introduces a new live-action iteration of villain M. Bison, and the actor who plays him might look familiar to DC fans.
body: The main antagonist of the "Street Fighter" series is M. Bison, crime boss of the Shadaloo organization, who dresses like a military dictator. In "Street Fighter" video games and animation, numerous voice actors have played Bison, from Canadian actor Richard Newman ("Beast Wars") in the West to Norio Wakamoto ("Dragon Ball Z," "Cowboy Bebop") in "Street Fighter" parent company Capcom's native Japan.

M. Bison has also been brought to live action in three "Street Fighter" films. The late Raul Julia (best known as Gomez Addams in the 1990s "Addams Family" films) played Bison in the 1994 "Street Fighter" film. In fact, it was Julia's last film role before his death, and he's widely considered the best part of the movie. Neal McDonough played the villain in 2009's "Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li," though without the character's famous outfit. In the new 2026 "Street Fighter" film (which includes a tribute to Julia), Bison is played by David Dastmalchian, an actor skilled at both comedy and playing genuinely disturbed villains.

articles.title: Deathstroke's Canceled DCEU Movie Storylines Explained By Joe Manganiello
articles.summary: According to Joe Manganiello, he was lined up to play Deathstroke in multiple DC Extended Universe movie storylines that were ultimately canceled.
body: Joe Manganiello has revealed the unrealized plans for his Deathstroke, aka Slade Wilson, in the DC Extended Universe. Often referred to as the Snyderverse, the DCEU came before James Gunn and Peter Safran took over as the heads of DC Studios. Ben Affleck wanted Deathstroke for his canceled "Batman" film, but that didn't pan out. However, as Manganiello has now explained, many other ideas were on the table.

"I got to play the character again for, like, two minutes in the reshoots. And for the next six years, there were just project after project and call for my agent after call for my agent about, 'Oh yeah, they're going to use your character in this. You're going to be in this. You're going to be the villain in 'Aquaman 2.' You're going to be in 'Suicide Squad 2' with this director. No, this director. No, you versus Will Smith. Oh, it's going to be a standalone.' Am I lucky or unlucky?"

The "Suicide Squad" sequel lost Will Smith as Deadshot due to scheduling conflicts. Evidently, WB wanted to make a Deadshot vs. Deathstroke movie of some kind after that as well. But that didn't happen, nor was Deathstroke included in "Aquaman 2," which became "Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom."

articles.title: Inside Tubi’s Plan to Build an R.L. Stine Cinematic Universe
articles.summary: The children’s horror author, along with filmmaker Jem Garrard and Tubi’s VP of Original Scripted Content Josh Van Houdt on bringing 'Pumpkinhead' and its sequel to the screen, and the streamer's future with 'Afraid of Clowns' and 'The Babysitter.'
body: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

“We had a major discussion about the R.L. Stine brand, and if we were doing Pumpkinhead as TV-14 or TV-PG,” Van Houdt tells The Hollywood Reporter. “When I was talking to S&P, and we asked what we can show if we do TV-14, not TV-PG, my favorite response from them was, ‘You can do vegetable gore, but not regular gore.’ I was like, we can have pumpkin guts, but we can’t have blood. Great, we can work with this. Vegetable gore it is.”

For three decades, Hollywood has adapted Stine’s sprawling library of over 300 middle grade and young adult horror titles. “Back in the ’90s, when we started the Goosebumps TV show, I was writing a book a month, so I had no time to work on the show at all,” Stine tells THR. “But it was fun for me to see what other writers could do. They would take my story and then go off in their own directions with it. The same with movie adaptations.”

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Triumphs With $15M as ‘Street Fighter’ Wins Weekend
articles.summary: A24's Elizabeth Holmes documentary had audiences pumped, notching 2,000 sellout screenings and becoming the highest-grossing title in two decades for a release under 1,000 theaters.
body: Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything far outpaced box office expectations in its impressive opening as Street Fighter ended up victorious over the weekend.

After being made in secret over three years, You Can See Everything has maintained a sense of mystery through its intriguing marketing that followed its surprise premiere at Telluride. The film enjoyed more than 2,000 sellout screenings nationwide this weekend, and videos on social media showed lines snaking through cinemas. The audience skewed young, with 70 percent under age 35 for a crowd that was 55 percent male. It will add to its theater count next weekend and continues a hot year for A24, following such previous 2026 successes as Backrooms, The Drama and The Invite.

The film’s Oscar buzz is likely to increase as You Can See Everything boasts sterling word of mouth. It holds a 99 percent critics approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and a score of 98 from audiences, while standing as the highest-rated Letterboxd title ever at 4.8. THR critic Angie Han praised it as “smart, funny and full of surprises.”

articles.title: This Late '40s Western TV Series Features An Actor We Don't Talk About Today
articles.summary: William Boyd has the distinction of starring in the first Western TV series, but the actor and his show both seem mostly forgotten these days.
body: After John Ford pulled a legendary performance out of John Wayne in 1939's "Stagecoach," the once flailing genre was revitalized. Suddenly the Western moved out of "poverty row" and was taken seriously again. One man who straddled both sides of this seminal evolution of the genre was William Boyd, who in the 1930s and '40s played cowboy hero Hopalong Cassidy on the silver screen before bringing him to TV in yet another seminal moment for the Western. And yet you probably never heard of him.

Boyd's career stretched beyond his Western films. He started out as an extra in Cecil B. DeMille's 1920 comedy "Why Change Your Wife?" before re-teaming with DeMille for 1925's "The Road to Yesterday." This film proved to be his breakout role, and along with 1926's "The Volga Boatman" helped propel him to leading man status, allowing him to appear in some of the best films of the silent era. But by the early 1930s, having lost his contract, Boyd was struggling to maintain his standing. Soon, however, he'd land the role which revitalized his career and with which he became synonymous.
